newsitem.title: USA: Conn. Energy set to enter info-tech venture.
newsitem.headline: Conn. Energy set to enter info-tech venture.

text.p: Connecticut Energy Corp, seeking growth beyond its core gas business, is soon set to announce it will buy into an information technology company that can cater to the needs of a deregulated utility industry.

"We want to buy 10 to 15 percent pieces of software companies and help them customize their products to meet the needs of other utilities," J.R. Crespo, Connecticut Energy's president and chief executive officer, said in an interview.
"And we're close to a deal," he said, adding it would be inappropriate to comment further before the deal is final.

Software for managing electronic bulletin boards -- a federal requirement for posting interstate gas transmission capacity and fees -- service vehicle dispatching, inventory management, and new utility systems are all examples of what would fit under the umbrella of such ventures, Crespo said.
They would also fit a recent pattern for the company, as it reaches into the deregulated market for new revenue, drawing on its experience as a local gas distributor.
"We're a medium cap company. Given our size, we're not going into ventures looking for a payback five years down the road. We're looking for returns for our shareholders right away," Crespo said.

The company's sole business for years was selling gas through what is now its biggest subsidiary, Southern Connecticut Gas Co, which serves about 156,000 customers in a nearly uninterrupted band along the state's shore.

Gas sales still accounted for the bulk of Connecticut Energy's overall 1996 operating revenue, which hit $261.1 million for the fiscal year ended September 30, 1996, a 12.5 percent increase over the $232.1 million it posted in 1995.
The company last year moved 31.5 billion cubic feet (bcf) of gas through its system.

While Southern Connecticut Gas has seen steady annual sales growth of about two percent, its customers are predominantly residential in established neighborhoods, so the growth has come through home conversions from heating oil rather than an expanding residential or commercial base.
This is pushing the parent company to look hard at deregulated activities, Crespo said, so far spawning two strategic alliances with established energy service companies.

Connecticut Energy's subsidiary CNE Energy Services Group, Inc, started in 1995, is pursuing energy service packages for other New England utilities via a joint venture 49 percent owned by Louis Dreyfus Energy Services Inc.

CNE Energy has also launched Total Peaking Services (TPS), a venture which aims to use CNE's direct access to the state's three main gas pipelines and its 1.2 billion cubic feet liquefied natural gas storage facility to create an interstate winter gas peaking service.
The TPS venture is with Houston-based PanEnergy Corp, with CNE holding 51 percent and PanEnergy the rest.

"We recognize there will be big winners and big losers in this game," Crespo said, referring to the initial forays by local gas distributors into energy marketing and energy management packages. "But you can't ignore deregulation, and we intend to be aggressive in the new marketplace."

Connecticut Energy has posted a steady rise in earnings since 1989, gradually raising its dividend while whittling away at its payout average, now down to 77 percent, which means keeping more money in the company.
Crespo said any further reduction of the payout average likely would have to come from greater efficiency through improved technology.
Connecticut Energy's net income for fiscal 1996 was $15.17 million, or $1.70 a share, a 7.9 percent increase over the $14.06 million ($1.60/share) it netted in 1995.
